p: The tale is said to date back to the 14th century and probably originated in the Soomra period, between 1050 and 1350. It was first written down in the 16th century by Shah Abdul Karim of Bulri, the great-great-grandfather of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, in his Bayan ul Arifeen, known to Sindhis as Karim Jo Risalo. It also appears in two chronicles, the Tarikh-i Tahiri, compiled in 1621, and the Tuhfat-al-Kiram of 1766–67.

In the story as it is told, Marvi is a young Khaskheli girl of the Panhwar tribe, and her captor is Umar Soomro, then ruler of Umerkot, who wanted to marry her for her beauty. When she refused him she was held for several years in Umarkot Fort. She resists both the ruler's overtures and the temptation to live in the palace as a queen, preferring a simple rural life among her own village people.

In the Shah Jo Risalo the tale stands among seven popular tragic romances of Sindh, with Sassui Punnhun, Sohni Mehar, Lilan Chanesar, Noori Jam Tamachi, Sorath Rai Diyach and Momal Rano. Their heroines are commonly known as the Seven Queens of Sindh, or the seven heroines of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai. Marvi is regarded, for her courage, as a symbol of love for one's soil.

The story has been retold in modern forms. A film, Umar Marvi, directed by Shaikh Hassan and produced by Syed Hussain Ali Shah Fazlani, who also acted in it, was released on 12 March 1956 as the first Sindhi-language feature film made in Pakistan. The Pakistan Television Corporation broadcast a serial, Marvi, in 1993, which set the story in modern times. The Indian writer Ram Panjwani wrote a Sindhi play, Umar Marui, and a Sindhi song of Coke Studio's fifteenth season, Aayi Aayi, was inspired by the tale.
